summary: Describes using the HMAC construction with the SHA-1 hash as the authentication mechanism inside IPsec's ESP and AH. It parallels the HMAC-MD5 document with a different hash. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: IPsec protects a packet in two ways: encrypting it, and proving that nobody changed it on the way. RFC 2404 defines the second part, using HMAC with SHA-1. The result is a 96-bit check value that only the sender and the receiver can produce.

questions: why does hmac-sha-1-96 truncate to 96 bits
what key length does hmac-sha-1-96 use
how does hmac detect a modified ipsec packet
what is the authenticator field in ipsec
subtitle: How IPsec's ESP and AH use HMAC with SHA-1, cut to 96 bits, to prove a packet is genuine and unchanged.

tldr.problem: IPsec's ESP and AH need a way to prove that a packet really came from the expected sender and was not modified on the way.
tldr.mechanism: Each packet is stamped with an HMAC computed with SHA-1 and a secret key shared by the two ends. HMAC-SHA-1-96 produces 160 bits, and only the first 96 bits are stored in the packet.
tldr.outcome: The receiver recomputes the whole 160-bit value and compares the first 96 bits with what arrived. RFC 2404 is a Proposed Standard and reports no practical attacks against the scheme at the time of writing.

facts.label: Padding
facts.value: SHA-1 padding only, no implicit packet padding

today: RFC 2404 is a Proposed Standard published in November 1998, and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it. Its rules for HMAC-SHA-1-96 inside ESP and AH therefore remain the ones on record.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 2404 specifies HMAC-SHA-1-96 as an authentication mechanism inside IPsec's Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) and Authentication Header (AH). HMAC is a secret key algorithm: the two ends share a key that outsiders do not have.

The goal is that the packet is authentic and cannot be modified in transit. If only the source and the destination know the HMAC key, a correct HMAC proves that it must have been added by the source. The RFC points to other documents for the remaining pieces needed to implement ESP and AH, including the confidentiality mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC says how IPsec should prove a packet is real. It uses a shared secret key and a hash function to make a check value that only the two ends of the connection can produce.

sections.title: Algorithm and Mode
sections.content:
HMAC-SHA-1-96 works on 64-byte blocks of data. Padding follows the SHA-1 standard, so an implementation built to that standard needs no extra padding, and no implicit packet padding is required.

The algorithm produces a 160-bit authenticator value. That value can be truncated as described in RFC 2104, and support for a truncated value using the first 96 bits MUST be provided. When sending, the truncated value is stored in the authenticator field. When receiving, the entire 160-bit value is computed and its first 96 bits are compared with the stored value. No other authenticator lengths are supported.

The length of 96 bits was chosen because it is the default authenticator length in AH and it meets the security requirements described in RFC 2104.
sections.plainLanguage: The check value starts out 160 bits long, but only the first 96 bits are kept and sent. The receiver works out the full value again and checks that those same 96 bits match.

sections.title: Performance
sections.content:
The RFC quotes a study saying that HMAC performance is essentially that of the underlying hash function. At the time of writing, no detailed performance analysis had been done of SHA-1, of HMAC, or of HMAC combined with SHA-1.

RFC 2104 outlines an implementation modification that can improve per-packet performance without affecting interoperability.
sections.plainLanguage: Running this check costs about as much as running SHA-1 on its own. The RFC also points to a known shortcut in RFC 2104 that makes each packet a little cheaper to check.

sections.title: Keying Material
sections.content:
RFC 2104 does not fix a key length, but this RFC requires support for a fixed key length of 160 bits and forbids any other length. The reason given is that keys shorter than the authenticator length decrease security strength, while keys longer than the authenticator length do not significantly increase it.

The 160-bit key must be generated with a strong pseudo-random function. No weak keys for HMAC were known at the time of writing, and the RFC says this does not mean weak keys do not exist. If a set of weak keys is identified, those keys must be rejected, followed by a request for replacement keys or a newly negotiated security association.

For data origin authentication, the key distribution mechanism must ensure that unique keys are allocated and distributed only to the parties taking part in the communication. The RFC also notes that periodic key refreshment is a fundamental security practice: it reduces the information available to a cryptanalyst and limits the damage of an exposed key.
sections.plainLanguage: The secret key is exactly 160 bits long, and no other length is allowed. It must come from a strong random source and be known only to the two ends of the connection. Changing it from time to time is good practice.

sections.title: Interaction with the ESP Cipher Mechanism
sections.content:
HMAC-SHA-1-96 authenticates a packet; it does not encrypt it. The RFC states that at the time of writing there were no known issues that would prevent using HMAC-SHA-1-96 with any specific cipher algorithm.

For the general mechanism of obtaining keying material when multiple keys are needed for a single security association, for example one key for confidentiality and one for authentication, the RFC refers to the IPsec security architecture document.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC adds a check, not encryption. The check sits alongside whatever cipher the connection uses, and it can be combined with any of them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security of HMAC-SHA-1-96 rests on the strength of HMAC and, to a lesser degree, on the strength of SHA-1. At the time of writing there were no practical cryptographic attacks against it.

RFC 2104 states that for minimally reasonable hash functions a birthday attack is impractical. For a 64-byte block hash such as HMAC-SHA-1-96, an attack involving the successful processing of 2**80 blocks would be infeasible unless the underlying hash turned out to have collisions after a much smaller number of blocks, a hash with such weak collision resistance being generally considered unusable. RFC 2104 also discusses the extra security that truncating the hash provides, and specifications that include HMAC are strongly encouraged to truncate.

The RFC notes that SHA-1 was never developed to be used as a keyed hash algorithm, while HMAC met that criterion from the onset. It also observes that part of any cryptographic algorithm's strength lies in the correctness of the implementation, the security of the key management mechanism, the strength of the secret key, and correct behaviour in every participating system. RFC 2202 contains test vectors and example code to help verify an implementation.
sections.plainLanguage: The scheme was considered strong when it was written. Its safety depends on the key staying secret, on the code being correct, and on every participating system behaving properly, so the RFC points to published test cases for checking an implementation.

items.title: Algorithm
items.text: HMAC as specified in RFC 2104, using the SHA-1 hash of FIPS 180-1.

items.title: Value produced
items.text: 160 bits, of which only the first 96 bits are used.

items.title: Stored in the packet
items.text: The truncated 96-bit value goes into the authenticator field.

items.title: Check on receipt
items.text: The full 160 bits are computed again and the first 96 bits are compared.

items.title: Key
items.text: Exactly 160 bits, generated with a strong pseudo-random function.

items.title: Block size
items.text: 64 bytes, with SHA-1 padding and no implicit packet padding.
